raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the lifesaving benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding chronic transvenous leads, which are a major source of infection, venous occlusion, lead failure, and extraction risk [1]. The contemporary S-ICD consists of a left lateral pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous shocking electrode; it senses far-field electrograms and delivers high-energy shocks but does not provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or conventional antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [2]. Thus, its principal niche is prevention of sudden cardiac death in patients who need defibrillation but not pacing [3,4].

The rationale for an extravascular defibrillator is strengthened by long-term experience with transvenous systems. Lead defects accrue over time [27], and generator or system revisions increase complication risk [26,28]. Early S-ICD studies showed that fully subcutaneous sensing and defibrillation were feasible, with effective ventricular fibrillation conversion and acceptable perioperative safety [2,6,7]. Subsequent registries and pooled analyses confirmed high conversion efficacy for spontaneous and induced ventricular arrhythmias and low rates of lead-related systemic infection, endocarditis, and vascular complications [11-14,18].

Patient selection is central. The S-ICD is attractive for young patients, those with inherited arrhythmia syndromes, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, difficult venous access, prior device infection, or high lifetime lead-risk exposure [8,19,20]. Conversely, it is generally unsuitable for patients needing permanent pacing, resynchronization, or frequent ATP-terminable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening remains important because the device senses subcutaneous QRS and T-wave signals; failed screening is more likely with broad QRS complexes, marked repolarization abnormalities, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and some congenital or inherited conditions [9].

Implantation has evolved. Initial three-incision approaches have largely been replaced by two-incision and intermuscular generator placement, improving cosmesis and pocket stability. Operator experience matters: registry data demonstrated a learning curve, with early reductions in procedure time and complications as teams became familiar with tunneling, pocket location, and vector selection [15]. Imaging-based assessment also matters; the PRAETORIAN score formalized evaluation of generator and coil position to predict defibrillation success and guide repositioning when necessary [23]. Defibrillation testing has traditionally been performed at implant because the system lacks an intracardiac shocking vector, although observational data suggest that careful implant technique may identify low-risk cases [22].

The major historical limitation of the S-ICD has been inappropriate shock, especially from T-wave oversensing, myopotentials, and supraventricular tachycardia. Pre-implant screening, dual-zone programming, conditional discrimination zones, and exercise testing in selected patients reduce this risk [5,10]. Algorithmic advances have been important: morphology-based discrimination performed favorably in head-to-head testing with transvenous algorithms [5], and later filtering such as SMART Pass substantially reduced oversensing-related inappropriate therapy [16,17]. The UNTOUCHED trial, enrolling primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction and standardized programming, reported low inappropriate shock rates, supporting modern programming and sensing refinements [25].

Comparative evidence has matured. The PRAETORIAN randomized trial showed that the S-ICD was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, with fewer lead-related complications but more early inappropriate shocks in some settings [24]. The ATLAS randomized trial further supported the perioperative safety advantage of avoiding transvenous leads, particularly for lead-related complications, while emphasizing that the choice of system should be individualized [30]. These trials reframed the S-ICD not as a niche substitute but as a first-line option for many ICD-eligible patients without pacing indications.

Special populations illustrate both strengths and limits. In dialysis patients, the S-ICD avoids venous instrumentation and intravascular hardware, potentially reducing bacteremia-related device infection and preserving central veins [19]. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, it avoids transvenous leads in often young patients, but careful sensing screening is critical because large QRS/T-wave amplitudes may predispose to oversensing [20]. Hybrid strategies are emerging: communication between leadless pacemakers and S-ICD systems may eventually address the absence of pacing and ATP without reintroducing transvenous leads [29].

In summary, the S-ICD is an established alternative to the transvenous ICD for patients requiring defibrillation without pacing. Its advantages are anatomical: no intravascular lead, no endocardial hardware, and fewer lead-related long-term hazards. Its disadvantages are functional: no chronic pacing, no resynchronization, no standard ATP, and reliance on subcutaneous sensing. Modern screening, implantation technique, programming, and discrimination algorithms have narrowed early limitations. Future developments will likely focus on modular extravascular systems that combine defibrillation, leadless pacing, and ATP while preserving the core benefit of avoiding transvenous leads.
